EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured thunderstorm wind gust at Southern Illinois Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the lower 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in far Southern Illinois with DCAPE of 1000J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||With the system primarily tracking from Southeast Missouri to West Kentucky, the lone severe weather report in Illinois was golf ball size hail reported in Pulaski County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to golf ball size was reported in Mounds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the sixth consecutive month, much of the region experienced below normal precipitation, with deficits of 1 to 2 inches common during the month of January. Mean temperatures were above normal for much of autumn, but below normal during December and January. While precipitation was below normal for the month, a disturbance brought almost an inch of rainfall west of I-55, which led to modest improvement in the drought conditions. Elsewhere, the ongoing drought expanded across central and eastern Illinois. Streamflows, lake levels, and regional water tables remained well below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month. An early month disturbance brought almost an inch of rain, resulting in modest improvement in the drought by mid-January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 5 to 7 inches of snow across Menard County.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Roads were particularly bad near Glendale in Pope County, IL. Ice on rural roadways in Saline County, IL caused one vehicle to overturn with a person trapped. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

For the sixth consecutive month, much of the region experienced below normal precipitation, with deficits of 1 to 2 inches common during the month of January. Mean temperatures were above normal for much of autumn, but below normal during December and January. While precipitation was below normal for the month, a disturbance brought almost an inch of rainfall west of I-55, which led to modest improvement in the drought conditions. Elsewhere, the ongoing drought expanded across central and eastern Illinois. Streamflows, lake levels, and regional water tables remained well below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was ongoing at the start of the month. Continued below normal precipitation led to the Severe to Extreme drought persisting through the month.

Lake enhanced snow developed on January 25th with higher snowfall amounts across eastern Cook County.  Snowfall amounts there included 10.5 inches in the Chicago Loop; 9.1 inches in Garfield Park; 9.0 inches in Avondale and Bridgeport; 8.8 inches in Glenview and 8.5 inches in Logan Square.  Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 4.4 inches.

A strong cold front moved across northern Illinois during the morning of January 14th with a band of heavy snow and snow squalls. Wind gusts were between 40 mph and 50 mph with a few higher gusts, including a gust to 61 mph near Crescent City. Visibility was reported to be near zero in many locations. Snowfall amounts were generally between 1 and 2 inches and with temperatures falling below freezing as the snow began, roads became icy.  Hundreds of vehicle accidents were reported across northern Illinois.

A major winter storm impacted southern Illinois on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th. Along and south of Route 13 towards Interstate 24, a brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 8 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in areas that experienced mixing. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassable closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in Massac County, IL. Route 3, 127, and 146 in Alexander County, IL were all snow and ice covered, which led to the County Sheriff issuing an Emergency Travel Only Order due to all roads being too dangerous for travel. Interstate 57 in Williamson County, IL also experienced very difficult travel due to the snow while Jefferson County, IL near Mount Vernon had a multi-vehicle pileup that blocked the southbound side during the afternoon hours on the 25th.  The collision near milepost 92 involved seven vehicles, including a jackknifed truck-tractor semi-trailer that led to minor injures and traffic being diverted. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow, especially near Du Quoin in Perry County, IL where most secondary roads were also impassable. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures.

A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of southern Illinois. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Roads were particularly bad near Glendale in Pope County, IL. Ice on rural roadways in Saline County, IL caused one vehicle to overturn with a person trapped. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southern Illinois on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Williamson County, IL on the 26th. Northwest portions of southern Illinois and areas south of route 13 only experienced advisory criteria with values of -9 to -14. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the early morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Alexander, Pulaski, and Massac County, IL where wind chills warmed above -5 the morning of the 26th due to calmer winds.

For the sixth consecutive month, much of the region experienced below normal precipitation, with deficits of 1 to 2 inches common during the month of January. Mean temperatures were above normal for much of autumn, but below normal during December and January. While precipitation was below normal for the month, a disturbance brought almost an inch of rainfall west of I-55, which led to modest improvement in the drought conditions. Elsewhere, the ongoing drought expanded across central and eastern Illinois. Streamflows, lake levels, and regional water tables remained well below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month. An early month disturbance brought almost an inch of rain, resulting in modest improvement in the drought by mid-January.

Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, above normal precipitation occurred during March, with the official observation at Peoria recording 3.12 inches of precipitation which was 0.43 inches above normal. By late March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Peoria County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois during the afternoon of Sunday, March 15, 2026. The environment was characterized by high shear and weak instability. A line of storms swept across the state, producing scattered wind damage and eight tornadoes within the NWS Central Illinois coverage area.  The tornadoes occurred southeast of the I-72 corridor and all were rated EF-0 or EF-1. No injuries occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began on the east side of Nokomis in Montgomery County, producing widespread tree damage. The tornado continued northeast, crossing into Christian County north-northwest of the town of Ohlman. The tornado continued northeast, impacting Rosamond and producing roof and tree damage. It then curved east into Pana where it uprooted and snapped several large trees before dissipating. The tornado produced EF-1 damage in both counties, and it lasted a total of 14 minutes, spanning 13.6 miles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of March 15th, a QLCS moved through southern and south-central Illinois. Stronger segments of the QLCS produced wind damage across the region. The QLCS ended up producing 8 tornadoes while it passed through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado touched down on the Hillsboro Country Club where it produced minor damage to a home. The tornado then travelled northeast where it damaged trees, an outbuilding, and electrical poles. The tornado dissipated just north of White Ave west of Irving.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down near Irving Road and North 17th Ave where it blew over a farm auger and lofted debris nearly a half mile to the southwest. The tornado then hit Witt directly where it lofted a carport and damaged multiple roofs and trees in town. The tornado tracked along State Route 16 into Coalton where it nearly completely removed the roof of a mobile home. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado crossed from Mason County into southwestern Tazewell County south of the intersection of Jacobs Road and Nichols Road at 12:11 AM CDT March 11th.  The tornado continued northeastward to about 1 mile west of Green Valley where it snapped 8 power poles before dissipating at 12:15 AM CDT.

Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.

Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A steel post in a concrete setting was ripped out of the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down on Florida Court.

This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple small trees were snapped, a pine tree was blown over, and a fence was damaged.

Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois on Sunday, March 15, 2026, sending a robust cold front sweeping across the state during the evening. Following the cold frontal passage, much colder air moved into the region, resulting in rain changing to snow. Snow accumulations of 2 to 4 inches occurred across Knox and Stark counties, with lesser amounts to the south and east. Strong westerly wind gusts of 40-50 mph led to blowing snow and reduced visibility at times from Sunday evening through the day on Monday, March 16. This led to hazardous travel conditions, with numerous accidents and some road closures reported. The impacts were most pronounced on north-south roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blowing snow and strong wind gusts had produced blizzard conditions across Knox County during the evening of Sunday, March 15, through the afternoon of Monday, March 16. Blizzard criteria was no longer being met as of mid-afternoon on Monday, March 16, but patchy blowing snow and slick roadways continued, resulting in hazardous travel conditions. Portions of I-74 north of Galesburg remained closed into the evening due to accidents. Conditions gradually improved into the evening of Monday, March 16, as the winds weakened.

There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of reports of 1 to 2 inch hail came out of Bonfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois on Sunday, March 15, 2026, sending a robust cold front sweeping across the state during the evening. Following the cold frontal passage, much colder air moved into the region, resulting in rain changing to snow. Snow accumulations of 2 to 4 inches occurred across Knox and Stark counties, with lesser amounts to the south and east. Strong westerly wind gusts of 40-50 mph led to blowing snow and reduced visibility at times from Sunday evening through the day on Monday, March 16. This led to hazardous travel conditions, with numerous accidents and some road closures reported. The impacts were most pronounced on north-south roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulations of 1 to 3 inches were reported across the region, along with westerly wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph. This resulted in blowing snow, slick roadways, and reduced visibility. Numerous accidents were reported across the region, particularly along north-south oriented roads. Conditions gradually improved into the evening of Monday, March 16, as the winds weakened.

Blizzard conditions subsided Monday afternoon, but areas of blowing snow and slick roads persisted into Monday evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, blowing snow, and strong westerly wind gusts led to blizzard conditions across Knox County from the evening of Sunday, March 15th, through the afternoon of Monday, March 16th. Numerous accidents were reported across the county, including semi-trucks on I-74. This resulted in road closures of I-74 north of Galesburg. A cooperative observer in Galesburg measured four inches of snow. Despite the accidents, no injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large storm system moved across the Midwest March 15 to the 16th, initially bringing rain and thunderstorms to the area on the morning of the 15th. This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. Local news reported that most areas schools were closed and several Department of Transportation districts reported snow covered road ways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter snowfall reports ranged from 6.0 inches 1 mile north northeast of Davis to 10 inches in Freeport. There were widespread automated weather observation reports of visibilities between 1/2sm to 1sm along with frequent wind gusts between 45 to 55 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two outbuildings sustained roof damage, trees were snapped, power lines were blown down, and a grain bin was knocked over.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto a porch as a thunderstorm moved through Carbondale. Time was estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down northeast of the intersection of North 1800th Street and East 2000th Avenue about 2 miles north-northwest of Yale at 6:10 AM CDT.  The tornado tracked northeastward, damaging trees and destroying a barn south of the intersection of North 2000th Street and East 2100th Avenue before dissipating at 6:12 AM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down northeast of the intersection of County Road 2800 East and County Road 2000 North about 1 mile south-southeast of Forest City at 12:06 AM CDT March 11th.  The tornado tracked northeastward, overturning several irrigation pivots and snapping trees along its path before crossing into southwestern Tazewell County south of the intersection of Jacobs Road and Nichols Road at 12:11 AM CDT.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of central and eastern Kankakee County before moving into northwest Indiana. The most notable damage caused by this tornado in Kankakee County occurred in the Aroma Park area. This tornado began just north of W 3000S Road southwest of Kankakee, IL, about one mile east of State Route 115. The tornado intensified while traveling east-northeastward into the far southern section of the city of Kankakee in the vicinity of Route 45, where concentrated higher end EF-1 tree damage and structural damage was observed. The tornado intensified further while moving across E 2500S Road, destroying a two-story home and several metal farm buildings, consistent with EF-3 caliber wind speeds. Concentrated extreme tree damage was noted, with numerous large hardwood trees snapped, stubbed, or uprooted despite lacking leaves, likely due to extensive debris lofting in the area.|After crossing I-57 and the Kankakee River, the tornado rapidly increased in size, producing a swath of significant damage in and near northern portions of Aroma Park. In this area, multiple homes were heavily damaged to an estimated EF-2 intensity. The tornado's peak width occurred here and was estimated to be approximately 1550 yards. Ground survey and aerial imagery suggests that the tornado further intensified as it tracked east-southeast before crossing the Kankakee River again. Within a narrow 150-200 yard wide section along S. Sandbar Road to the northeast of Aroma Park, three homes were completely destroyed, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds, and multiple others were heavily damaged and rendered uninhabitable. A heavy pickup truck parked in front of the garage of one of the destroyed homes was moved over 100 feet into a ditch next to the driveway, possibly being spun around the remnants of a small tree before reaching the ditch. In addition, on the other side of Sandbar Road, a crossover type SUV appeared to have been rolled onto the adjacent property and deposited onto a pile of debris just north of a heavily damaged residence. Along the swath of the most intense structural damage, concentrated extreme tree damage was noted, with numerous large hardwood trees snapped, stubbed, or uprooted despite lacking leaves, likely owing to extensive flying debris. Along Sandbar Road and through the Kankakee Elks Golf Course, the tornado's width was estimated at near 1500 yards. The tornado then continued generally east to east-northeast towards the Indiana state line, downing numerous additional trees, causing occasional structural damage, and flipping irrigation pivots as it moved just north of the communities of Wichert and Hopkins Park. The tornado continued on its destructive path into Newton County, Indiana where it caused additional EF-3 damage before eventually lifting west of De Motte in Jasper County. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Aroma Park and the other two in Newton County, Indiana.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high-end EF2, possible multi-vortex, tornado with estimated peak winds around 130 mph started along Highway 20, southwest of Lena IL, and tracked through Lena before lifting just southwest of Orangeville. The tornado caused significant damage to trees along its path, including uprooting and snapping trees. When the tornado begun it immediately caused EF1 damage to trees, gaining strength to an EF2 tornado snapping many power poles southwest of Lena. The tornado turned to the right, into town causing a lot of roof damage and tree damage. A lot of houses had shingle and siding damage. The most significant damage occurred on Grove Street, where three houses lost their entire roof structure. Two of the homes experienced partial exterior wall collapses. Damage in this area is consistent with 130 MPH winds. In Lena, the damage footprint in Lena is approximately 1250 yards wide. As the tornado moved to the northeast, damage to farm structures was noted. Even towards the end of the path, the tornado was causing EF1 damage to trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms moved across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois and produced 50+ mph winds, causing some areas of damage to trees, roofs, and a few outbuildings.  The line of very gradually fading storms produced surges of straight-line wind damage. These were most pronounced to the immediate south of mesovortices (small scale circulations within the thunderstorm line that can in themselves result in tornadoes). Based on the nature of damage, observations, and radar, these reflect 65-80 mph wind gusts.||Two main areas of damage that experienced enhanced wind surges were:  1.) Kalona, IA (Washington Co)  and 2.) the east-southeast side of Iowa City (Johnson County).||A third area of isolated wind damage from Miles to Sabula, IA (Jackson County) was a little different in that it was much more of an outflow surging from decaying storms, but again straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Recorded with an anemometer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The EF1 tornado with winds up to 95 mph appeared to start just south of County Road 2200 N in Bureau County, where a barn structure sustained roofing damage. The tornado then moved northeastward into LaSalle County, producing damage to trees and farm outbuildings. Several wooden power poles were damaged just southeast of Mendota before a semi truck was blown over on I-39 as the tornado continued northeastward. The tornado then passed near Meriden, causing additional damage to trees and farm outbuildings before dissipating in an open field northwest of Earlville.

During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in far eastern Whiteside County just north of Fulfs Road and just west of the Whiteside-Lee county line, where satellite imagery showed the beginning of a narrow southwest-northeast path of disturbed soil through farm fields. Drone footage taken along Mound Hill Road in Lee County revealed swirl marks in the field to the west that aligned with the path that was evident in the satellite imagery, confirming that the tornado remained on the ground continuously as it tracked into Lee County. The tornado crossed Mound Hill Road, downing a number of power poles and impacting a property on the east side of the road. The tornado reached its peak intensity here, destroying multiple outbuildings and snapping several trees at this property. The tornado left additional swirl marks in a field to the northeast of the property before causing damage to trees, a residence, and a metal outbuilding along and just south of Lenox Road. As the tornado reached Timber Creek Road, it caused damage to a barn, at least one power pole, and several trees. On the north side of the road, the tornado pushed an old barn off of its foundation into a grain leg, causing the grain leg to collapse. A concrete silo was also toppled at the same location. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing tree and roof damage at a property along Peek Home Road, then damaging an outbuilding, a house, and more trees at a property at Penrose Road and Swarts Road. The tornado produced its last instance of damage at the Hey Tree Service facility along U.S. Route 52/State Route 26 southeast of Woosung before dissipating prior to reaching the Ogle County line. Straight-line wind damage was also observed to the south and east of the tornado's track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-month precipitation deficit from Fall of 2025 to February of 2026 led to widespread Severe Drought (D2) conditions developing across central Illinois. However, above normal rainfall during March 2026 led to substantial improvements in the drought conditions, to the point that only a few counties had lingering Severe Drought entering the month of April. A continued active pattern led to the eradication of Severe Drought area-wide early in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month as the result of a multi-month precipitation deficit spanning October 2025 to February 2026. However, above normal precipitation occurred in March and the active pattern persisted into early April. The cooperative observer in Normal measured 3.14 inches of precipitation during the first week of April, which nearly exceeded the average precipitation for the entire month (3.72). The continued wet conditions led to Severe Drought ending.

Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado formed briefly in the occlusion of an rear flank downdraft northwest of Pearl City. It heavily damaged and destroyed several farm outbuildings, lifted a large farm wagon into an outbuilding, damaging the roof and side. The tornado also snapped several tree trunks and tree damage. Power poles were also snapped as the tornado crossed Illinois Highway 73 before lifting shortly thereafter. The tornado caused EF-1 damage with maximum estimated winds of 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-month precipitation deficit from Fall of 2025 to February of 2026 led to widespread Severe Drought (D2) conditions developing across central Illinois. However, above normal rainfall during March 2026 led to substantial improvements in the drought conditions, to the point that only a few counties had lingering Severe Drought entering the month of April. A continued active pattern led to the eradication of Severe Drought area-wide early in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month as the result of a multi-month precipitation deficit spanning October 2025 to February 2026. However, above normal precipitation occurred in March and the active pattern persisted into early April. The continued wet conditions led to Severe Drought ending.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The environment during the afternoon of April 17th was primed for the development of severe thunderstorms. One thunderstorm split into two in Missouri. The left split passed through Pike and Brown counties where it consistently caused wind damage along its path.

In Pittsfield, a power pole was snapped off on the 200 block of North Illinois Street. Several trees were downed here. Griggsville incurred more structural damage, with a home sustained roof damage, part of a metal roof torn from an outbuilding, power poles snapped, and a large carport structure collapsed onto a combine to the northeast of town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The body of a middle-aged man was recovered from Lake Michigan at Openlands Lakeshore Preserve in Highland Park on the evening of the 17th. It's also worth noting that dense fog was present on the lake from the evening of the 16th into the morning of the 17th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was confirmed via storm chaser video. No damage occurred, so an intensity rating could not be assigned.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of far northern Illinois during the evening of April 14th producing large hail, wind damage.  Flash flooding also occurred in parts of the Chicago metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread street and basement flooding was reported across much of northern Chicago, including Edison Park, Norwood Park, Jefferson Park, Rogers Park, Edgewater, Uptown, Forest Glen, North Park and West Ridge. Lakeshore Drive was flooded near Montrose Beach. The underpass on Interstate 94 at Pratt Avenue in Lincolnwood was flooded. In Edison Park, cars were reported stalled with water up to their bumpers.  Multiple roads and viaducts were flooded in Rosemont and near O'Hare Airport, including along portions of Interstate 90.  Rainfall amounts included 3.46 inches in Harwood Heights; 2.66 inches in Rogers Park; 2.59 inches in Park Ridge and 2.56 inches in Lincolnwood. Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 2.43 inches, which was a record 24 hour total for April 14th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began near the intersection of Freeport Road and Bates Road southeast of Harrison, initially downing several tree branches at and near a small cemetery. The tornado produced additional tree damage as it tracked eastward along Roscoe Road before entering the west side of Roscoe and reaching its peak intensity as it tracked through the Hawks Point, Crystal Hills, and Oxford Commons subdivisions. There, multiple homes had portions of their roofs torn off or damaged and had sections of siding and fascia peeled off. A few homes also had their garage doors blown in, leading to parts of their garage walls getting blown out in a few cases. Numerous trees were also uprooted or damaged in these subdivisions. The tornado then continued eastward, knocking down several power poles along Gleasman Road and damaging a nearby farm outbuilding before crossing the Rock River. East of the Rock River, the tornado continued to cause extensive tree damage. Multiple additional houses sustained roof and fascia damage from the tornado as well. The tornado appeared to dissipate just as it reached the Winnebago-Boone County line. Extensive straight-line wind damage was also observed in close proximity to the tornadic circulation, particularly along its southern flank.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado appeared to touch down in an open field southwest of the intersection of E 1200 North Road and N 2450 East Road and impacted a farm, leading to damage to several structures. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing damage to trees and farm outbuildings. The peak intensity of the tornado occurred near the end of the path along the Iroquois and Newton County border, where over a dozen new wooden power poles were snapped at their base. The tornado then appeared to lift just northeast of US-24 in southwestern Newton County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several videos were shared of a slow-moving landspout tornado that occurred a few miles east of Beaverville and north northeast of Donovan in rural northeast Iroquois County. No known damage was reported.

Rainfall amounts included 2.63 inches in Mount Prospect; 2.62 inches two miles east of Schaumburg and 2.10 inches in Elk Grove Village.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high-end EF-1 tornado began near Meridian Road between Favor Road and Steward Road southeast of Harrison, initially causing damage to trees and an outbuilding. Video footage from storm chasers documented the tornado becoming fully condensed and growing in size and intensity as it tracked east-northeastward across Favor Road and impacted two farmsteads, causing significant damage to a few outbuildings and snapping and uprooting multiple trees. Additional storm chaser footage showed the tornado intensifying again as it tracked northeastward across Gummow Road and then reaching peak intensity as it impacted a property along Freeport Road. At this property, the majority of an older two-story house's roof was removed, several trees were snapped, and an old barn was destroyed. The footage then captured the tornado making a sharp turn to the southeast and crossing Freeport Road once again before roping out and eventually dissipating in open fields near Owen Center Road.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to half-dollar size fell west of Browns.

Drought continued into May in far southern Illinois.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.

A deep low pressure system was positioned north of the Great Lakes on May 4th, with a cold front extending southwestward into Iowa. Ahead of the front, sustained southwesterly gradient winds of 20-30mph with gusts as high as 40 to 45mph resulted in plumes of blowing dust. The dust led to near-zero visibility in spots, severely impacting travel and leading to at least one road closure in central Illinois. A track meet in Macon County was also cancelled due to the conditions. No traffic accidents were reported during this dust episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A plume of blowing dust impacted portions of Macon County, severely reducing visibility to near-zero at times. Broadcast media shared a photo of dust blowing across IL-121 between Latham and Warrensburg. A security camera west of Warrensburg also showed reduced visibility. Similar conditions were reported in Maroa, where a track meet was cancelled due to the dust storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant tree damage occurred at Walnut Ridge Cemetery on the north side of Virginia.
